hook: A shambles was a real place, and you could buy meat there.
modernAnchor: A wrecked kitchen, a collapsed plan, a room the morning after. We call it a shambles.
journey: Old English sceamol meant a bench or a footstool, taken from Latin scamellum, a little bench.
Butchers laid their meat out on those benches, and by the 1300s a shambles was the row of stalls where meat was sold. Some English towns still have a street called the Shambles.
Where meat was sold, animals were killed, and the word slid off the counter and into the slaughterhouse behind it.
From a slaughterhouse it became any scene that resembled one, and from there, any mess at all.
